overview: These Arakan snapshots belong to the region’s early cities and competing royal lineages, especially Vesali. They are not evidence of one uninterrupted dynasty. The 600 to 700 outline omits Vesali itself; the 900 to 1000 outline includes it but is still approximate. Objects below come from different parts of the first millennium, with later evidence identified explicitly.

periods.title: Cities and regional connections
periods.summary: Vesali’s buildings, coinage and religious institutions belong to a wider early-medieval setting.

periods.title: Later inscriptions and uncertain political succession
periods.summary: The sequence and absolute dates of rulers remain disputed.

items.text: The early cities stood in the Kaladan and Lemro lowlands, within a restricted strip suitable for irrigated rice growing. Hills surrounded this productive land on three sides, while river mouths connected it to the sea. Farmers and water management helped support the settlements behind the royal monuments.

Vesali stood beside a watercourse leading into the Kaladan and onward to the Bay of Bengal. Its oval enclosure contained a smaller, roughly rectangular walled area, interpreted as a royal citadel. Rivers made journeys and exchanges possible; the archaeological plan shows where people invested labor in organizing the city.

A Niticandra silver coin in the British Museum is 32 millimeters across and weighs 7.41 grams. Its resting bull wears a garland; sun and moon appear on the other side. The catalogue dates it to 499 to 554, before these snapshots, although the dynasty’s absolute chronology is debated. Tiny objects can preserve wonderfully deliberate details.

A hoard found at Hsindet in 1985 contained coins of Arakan rulers together with two Pyu coins. Its location lay on a route toward Sriksetra. Islam and Cribb interpret the mixed contents as evidence of connections between the regions; the coins alone cannot identify the people who carried them.

The dates written beside ancient kings in modern books are sometimes less secure than they look. Islam and Cribb compare Arakan coins with better-dated issues elsewhere and propose a later chronology than traditional lists. This is why the card avoids assigning every ruler a precise reign or turning the map’s gaps into dynastic collapses.

sections.title: A monastery needed dishes, needles and labor

items.text: The Prine Cha inscription, probably eighth or ninth century, includes the Sanskrit word “śākabhājanatrayaṁ”: “three vegetable platters”. This is a scholarly Roman transliteration of its Siddhamatrika-type script, not the original letter shapes. Alongside a water pot and other vessels, the phrase makes monastic life wonderfully tangible: meals needed dishes.

The same later inscription lists five sewing needles and what Griffiths tentatively interprets as a stand for a wooden washboard. Robes required repair and washing as well as religious ceremony. The washboard identification is uncertain, but the needles provide a clear reminder that clothes did not mend themselves.

The monastery’s donated resources also included two buffaloes and an enslaved person. The inscription associates the endowment with a king’s elder brother. Religious generosity rested partly on control over land, goods and people; this record preserves unequal social relationships alongside its concern for merit.

A bell inscription from Vesali dedicates a Buddhist monk’s gift for the benefit of his parents, teachers and all beings. This middle-first-millennium witness links religious giving with family gratitude and learning. It records an aspiration expressed by a donor, rather than a description of every household’s beliefs.

Anandacandra’s later royal inscription credits him with wells, causeways and regular activity in a dining hall. These claims show that providing water and supporting collective meals could be part of a king’s public reputation. They do not establish a universal welfare system or a citywide sewer network.

The same royal account mentions a princess, Dhenda, arriving through a diplomatic marriage and gifts sent to monks in the land of King Silamegha, including robes and a female elephant. Such exchanges linked courts and religious communities. The inscription celebrates those relationships from the Arakan ruler’s perspective.

Gutman’s study notes that Anandacandra supported Brahman institutions as well as Buddhist foundations. His record describes land, servants, musical instruments and musicians attached to those establishments. Religious patronage employed many kinds of work, from maintaining buildings to performing music, beyond the king and the people conducting rituals.

Sanskrit inscriptions and Pali religious passages show connections with learned traditions around the Bay of Bengal. These surviving texts document specialists able to compose, copy or recite religious material. They do not reveal how many ordinary children attended lessons, or which languages families used around their own cooking fires.

The Anandacandra pillar preserves different inscriptions on different faces. The clearer royal eulogy can be read much more fully than some earlier and later writing. Repeated use made the stone a record of changing authorities; worn letters explain why its history still requires patient comparison rather than a tidy list of dates.

A Vesali gateway timber produced a calibrated date of 1260 to 1400 CE, centuries after these snapshots. Hudson cautions that one date cannot settle the city’s whole history, but it indicates later building activity. An old city could acquire a new gate long after the kings remembered on its coins.

ending.text: Neither 700 nor 1000 is a demonstrated disappearance of Arakan’s inhabitants. Political centers and ruling houses changed, and later settlements flourished along the Lemro River. Vesali’s later gate timber also warns against imagining a single final abandonment. These snapshots leave gaps in map coverage, not blank centuries in people’s lives.
